issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with a toxic chemical exposure trauma. The selected Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/being-followed danger themes ('someone is following me', lock checking) rather than contamination, health deterioration, environmental exposure, or bodily harm themes that would fit chemical exposure.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategy item 'Never Alone' is also strongly interpersonal/assault-focused and is hard to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure. 'Avoid Conflict' similarly targets confrontation rather than exposure-related danger, and is not plausibly linked to the selected Threat items or trauma type.

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'Never Alone with another person' is hard to reconcile clinically: it implies fear of interpersonal danger rather than contamination, bodily harm, or environmental exposure. No Trigger, Memory, or Appraisal items support an interpersonal-assault formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Conflict' also points to interpersonal threat management rather than consequences of chemical exposure. With no corroborating interpersonal threat, appraisal, or memory content, this strategy appears misaligned with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, avoiding conflict is not a plausible trauma-linked maladaptive strategy unless supported by appraisals about blame, authority, or interpersonal danger, which are absent here. It appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette: Fifteen months ago, Duy was working on a rooftop cooling tower at a downtown logistics warehouse when a high-pressure refrigerant line cracked without warning. A dense, sweet-smelling vapor rolled across the grating, stinging his eyes and burning his throat before he could pull his disposable mask tighter. A hazmat crew pulled him clear, and though his lungs healed, his nervous system never reset. A visceral certainty took hold: invisible threats could fill a room without warning, and nothing was truly sealed against them. Over the following months, Duy’s body never stopped bracing for the next exposure. His shoulders remained permanently knotted, his jaw clenched, and his breath stayed shallow, as if his physiology was still trying to filter a toxic atmosphere that wasn’t there. When he returned to his own home, he found himself pacing the perimeter at night, turning each deadbolt three times and lifting every window sash to verify it was sealed. When his wife would rest her hand on his shoulder and tell him the air inside was perfectly clean, Duy would nod politely but feel nothing but a cold, impenetrable certainty in his chest. He had come to believe that reassurance was just another layer of paint over a leak, and that silence from others did not mean safety—it only meant the threat had not yet announced itself. Because his body stayed locked in that perpetual state of alarm, Duy slowly began to construct a life that kept the pressure valves from ever rising again. The constant physiological readiness made stillness unbearable; the moment he allowed himself to relax on the couch, a terrifying certainty took hold that his guard was down and an unseen vapor would slip through a seal he no longer trusted. He began avoiding rooms where he could not see an exit, and he started turning down work assignments that required navigating tight mechanical rooms. He avoided stressors of any kind, recalibrating his schedule to eliminate urgency, skipping overtime, and quietly requesting lateral transfers. As the weeks turned to months, the certainty that the air was untrustworthy only deepened, and the avoidance behaviors only grew stricter. Every time he skipped a stressful shift or checked a lock one more time, the temporary relief confirmed his worst fear: he had to keep his guard up forever, and the loop of suspicion and restriction only widened. At work, this recalibration became impossible to hide. As an HVAC technician who spent his days crawling through ceiling plenums and kneeling beside roaring compressors, Duy found himself unable to enter the narrow access tunnels where the air grew stale and heavy. He began claiming he could not fit in the ductwork and refused to work near chemical storage rooms. His foreman grew frustrated as Duy’s reliability eroded, noting how he would sit in the open garage for hours instead of going upstairs to watch television with his wife. His spouse soon realized he was no longer sleeping in the guest room without a space heater and a cracked window, and she began interpreting his flinches at the central air handler’s mechanical rumble as proof that he was slowly strangling their life together. By the time he finally walked into the clinic, Duy’s PCL-5 score of seventy-three was no longer just a number—it was the sum of sixteen months spent bracing for an invisible cloud that never left. What brought him through the door was not a single crisis, but the quiet exhaustion of watching his own world shrink. He had stopped driving past industrial parks, he could barely sit through dinner with friends when they mentioned their new home renovation, and he no longer trusted his own breathing. He sat in the therapist’s chair now, hands resting flat on his knees to keep them from reaching for the door handle, hoping the session might finally offer him a way to believe the air around him was just air again.
